content: The text provided is a long list of references, guidelines, and contributors related to medical and public health topics, particularly focusing on delayed umbilical cord clamping, maternal and infant health, nutrition, and related ethical and procedural considerations. 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on delayed umbilical cord clamping, emphasizing its benefits for improving maternal and infant health and nutritional outcomes. These guidelines are accessible through the WHO's official website and were last accessed on June 18, 2014. 2. Blouin et al. conducted a study in the Peruvian Amazon to evaluate the impact of a two-component intervention aimed at shifting hospital practices from early to delayed umbilical cord clamping. The findings were published in the Revista Panamericana de Salud Pública in 2011, highlighting the clinical implications of this practice. 3. Another study by Blouin et al. explored the timing of umbilical cord clamping in relation to infant anemia and the role of maternal anemia. This research, published in Paediatrics International Child Health in 2013, underscores the importance of maternal health in determining neonatal outcomes. 4. The WHO's 2014 guideline on delayed umbilical cord clamping provides evidence-based recommendations to enhance maternal and infant health and nutrition. This document is available on the WHO's nutrition database and was last accessed on September 9, 2014. 5. Ethical considerations in medical practice are discussed in the work of Andre and Velasquez (1987), titled What is Ethics? This foundational text addresses key issues in medical ethics. 6. Beauchamp and Childress's seminal book, Principles of Biomedical Ethics (6th edition, 2008), provides a comprehensive framework for ethical decision-making in healthcare, including principles such as autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice. 7. The WHO Regional Office for Europe issued a declaration in 1994 promoting patients' rights in Europe, emphasizing the importance of ethical and equitable healthcare delivery. 8. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, a pivotal document in global child health and rights, was accessed in January 2015 to inform policies and practices. 9. Gillon's 1994 article in the BMJ discusses the four principles approach to medical ethics, advocating for a balanced consideration of ethical principles in clinical practice. 10. Braveman and Gruskin (2003) define health equity in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, emphasizing the need for fairness and justice in health outcomes. 11. Schrecker et al. (2010) explore how human rights can advance health equity in the global marketplace, as published in Social Science & Medicine. 12. Braveman et al. (2011) argue that addressing health disparities is fundamentally an issue of justice, as detailed in the American Journal of Public Health. 13. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) issued Committee Opinion No. 399 in 2008, discussing the ethical and practical considerations of umbilical cord blood banking. 14. Rucinski et al. (2010) investigated the opinions and beliefs of Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black women regarding cord blood donation, with findings published in Transfusion. 15. Samuel and Kerridge (2007) examined emerging ethical issues in umbilical cord blood banking in Australia, as published in the Journal of Bioethical Inquiry. 16. The WHO's expert advisory panels and committees provide guidance on various health topics, with documents accessible through the WHO's official website. 17. Mathai, Gülmezoglu, and Hill (2014) reviewed WHO recommendations for preventing postpartum hemorrhage, emphasizing evidence-based practices. 18. The Cochrane Collaboration provides systematic reviews of healthcare interventions, with resources available through their official website. 19. Guyatt et al. (2011) introduced the GRADE guidelines, which offer a systematic approach to evaluating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations in clinical practice. 20. The WHO's 47th edition of Basic Documents outlines the organization's foundational principles and policies, accessible through their website. 21. WHO guidelines for managing postpartum hemorrhage and retained placenta provide critical recommendations for improving maternal outcomes. 22. Ongoing clinical trials, such as the PREMOD trial and the Australian Placental Transfusion Study, investigate the effects of delayed cord clamping and other related practices on neonatal health outcomes. 23. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development includes experts in various fields, such as maternal and child health, nutrition, and public health, who contribute to the development of evidence-based recommendations. 24. External resource experts, including academics, clinicians, and public health professionals, collaborate with the WHO to ensure the scientific rigor and applicability of its guidelines. 25. The WHO regional offices and their advisors play a crucial role in implementing health policies and programs tailored to the needs of specific regions. 26. The WHO guideline development group for nutrition actions (2013–2014) included experts in epidemiology, program implementation, and systematic reviews, ensuring a multidisciplinary approach to guideline formulation. 27. The WHO's delayed umbilical cord clamping guideline highlights the importance of this practice in improving health outcomes for mothers and infants, supported by extensive research and expert consensus. 28. Contributors to the WHO guidelines include technical officers, medical officers, and consultants specializing in areas such as nutrition, public health, and maternal and child health. 29. The WHO's commitment to advancing global health is reflected in its comprehensive guidelines, expert panels, and collaborative efforts with international organizations and researchers.
